title: ServiceAccounts – Pod Passports 📇
description: Understand how Pods authenticate to the Kubernetes API using ServiceAccounts.

slides.title: Every Pod Has an Identity 🆔
slides.content:
# Meet the ServiceAccount

When you create a Pod, Kubernetes automatically assigns a **ServiceAccount** to it. If you don’t specify one, the `default` ServiceAccount in the Pod’s namespace is used.

A ServiceAccount:
- Is a Kubernetes object (kind: ServiceAccount)
- Provides a **token** (JWT) that the Pod can use to authenticate to the API
- Can be restricted with RBAC to limit what the Pod can do

slides.title: ServiceAccount Resources 📜
slides.content:
## See what’s there

```bash
kubectl get serviceaccounts
kubectl describe serviceaccount default
```

Every namespace has a `default` ServiceAccount. It has no special permissions by itself – it’s just an identity. Permissions come from RBAC bindings.

quizData.question: True or False: The default ServiceAccount has admin powers in its namespace.
quizData.explanation: It has no special rights; RBAC must explicitly grant permissions.

slides.title: How Pods Use a ServiceAccount 🔑
slides.content:
## The token gets mounted

When a Pod starts, the kubelet:
1. Projects a **service account token** (JWT) into the Pod at `/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token`.
2. Also provides the API server address and CA certificate.
3. The Pod can use that token in an `Authorization: Bearer` header to call the API.

In newer clusters, **token projection** is used; the token is volume‑mounted with a limited lifetime.

slides.title: Creating a Dedicated ServiceAccount 🛠️
slides.content:
## Don’t use default for apps

```bash
kubectl create serviceaccount app-sa
```

Then reference it in your Pod spec:
```yaml
spec:
  serviceAccountName: app-sa
```

This gives that Pod its own identity, which you can then lock down with RBAC.

quizData.question: Which field in a Pod spec assigns a ServiceAccount?
quizData.explanation: `spec.serviceAccountName` sets the ServiceAccount for the Pod.

slides.title: Disabling Auto‑Mount of Tokens 🛑
slides.content:
## If your Pod doesn’t need API access

For security, prevent the token from being mounted at all:
```yaml
spec:
  automountServiceAccountToken: false
```

Even better, set it on the ServiceAccount itself, and it will apply to all Pods using it. This reduces the attack surface.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Use tokenRequest API for short‑lived tokens

Instead of mounting a static token, you can request a time‑bound token via the API, enhancing security. Many SDKs support this natively.
